The evidence base is disease-specific observational cohorts and registries, so individual claims require dated physiatric, orthopedic, cardiology, sleep, swallow, or densitometric review with competing-cause exclusion, and review by a qualified medical professional.

Pathway and duplicate-scope screens - intermediate-node guard: no -> congestive-heart-failure or cardiac-arrhythmia edge (WITHHELD - intermediate-node: the cardiomyopathy identity's published windows carry both pathways and this identity routes through cardiomyopathy; ME-29 no recycling); no -> respiratory-failure edge (no catalog identity; the located respiratory material is recorded as context on the sleep-apnea edge); no -> cognitive-disorder edge (WITHHELD - constitutive/developmental proximity: cognitive impairment in Duchenne is part of the primary phenotype from dystrophin-deficient brain isoforms rather than a secondary condition, and no condition-specific downstream quantification was located); no -> visual-impairment or epilepsy edge (zero located condition-specific quantification); no -> obesity edge (no catalog identity; corticosteroid-associated weight gain recorded as a pathway component on the sleep-apnea edge); ME-29 sibling discipline - the als dysphagia window, cerebral-palsy scoliosis window, joint-replacement and burns contracture windows, and hypogonadism osteoporosis window keep their own evidence and none is recycled.
governanceNotes: D1 batch 62 (2026-09-26): six bounded association edges authored - muscular-dystrophy to contractures (rank 1), to scoliosis (rank 2), to cardiomyopathy (rank 3), to sleep-apnea (rank 4), to dysphagia (rank 5), and to osteoporosis (rank 6) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true. The contracture proposition rests on the 178-boy longitudinal cohort (PMID 35124659) and the 33-boy maturation-corrected trajectory study (PMID 40100909). The scoliosis proposition rests on the MD STARnet population-based study (PMID 34787322) and the 105-patient natural-history review (PMID 3611341). The cardiomyopathy proposition rests on the 33-patient adult cohort (PMID 42112505), the 274-patient HOPE-MD registry (PMID 42169468), and the CMR review (PMID 41548716). The sleep-apnea proposition rests on the 12-patient polysomnography cohort (PMID 32740854) and the sleep-disordered-breathing review (PMID 28397169). The dysphagia proposition rests on the 48-patient adult cohort (PMID 37212070) and the 206-person orofacial database (PMID 42142020). The osteoporosis proposition rests on the 408-patient imaging cohort (PMID 41912872) and the vertebral-fracture risk-factor study (PMID 36342539).

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-26: (i) treatment-era and treatment-mediation limits - glucocorticoid exposure modifies every anchor (scoliosis hazards lower with steroid use; osteoporosis jointly driven by steroids and disuse; cardiomyopathy course altered by early cardioprotection) and the osteoporosis edge asserts a MULTIFACTORIAL mechanism naming both documented contributors; (ii) subtype scope - all anchors are Duchenne/Becker specific and other dystrophies are explicitly out of scope; (iii) phenotype boundary - cognitive impairment is treated as part of the primary Duchenne phenotype rather than a secondary condition; (iv) outcome-measure limits - the dysphagia anchors are patient-reported and screening measures, the sleep anchor is 12 patients, and the cardiomyopathy registry is conditioned on established systolic dysfunction; (v) sibling-window discipline - the als, cerebral-palsy, joint-replacement, burns, hypogonadism, and cardiomyopathy-family windows keep their own evidence and none is recycled (ME-29).

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Duchenne muscular dystrophy documents progressive joint contractures at longitudinal cohort level: the 178-boy longitudinal cohort with annual range-of-motion measurement at hip, knee, and ankle found contracture prevalence and severity increasing with age and more severe contractures significantly associated with worse ambulatory function, with contracture severity moderately predicted by MRI muscle fat fraction and T2 (PMID 35124659), and the 33-boy maturation-corrected trajectory study found dorsiflexion range of motion declining 0.23-0.33 z-score per year after ages 6.6-9.4 alongside muscle size loss (PMID 40100909); the relationship is recorded as documented disease-sequela association only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: the anchors are Duchenne-specific observational cohorts where contractures develop alongside progressive myopathy, glucocorticoid exposure, and ambulation loss, so whether any individual contracture is attributable to the dystrophy requires individual physiatric attribution with immobilization, orthopedic, and neurologic exclusion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Progressive dystrophin-deficient muscle degeneration with fibrofatty replacement drives loss of muscle extensibility and agonist-antagonist imbalance so adaptive muscle-tendon shortening and fixed joint contractures result, the shortening route consistent with contracture severity tracking age, fat fraction, and functional decline in the longitudinal cohort, but whether this route produced any individual contracture remains hypothesized until range-of-motion and imaging records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at single-disease longitudinal cohort class only: both anchors are Duchenne-specific small-to-moderate cohorts (178 and 33 boys), the 178-boy study found muscle fat fraction and T2 only moderately predict contracture, implying tendon and joint capsule contributions unmeasured here, and both cohorts are glucocorticoid-era with treatment modifying the natural history.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: No located cohort separates dystrophy-driven shortening from immobilization and positioning effects; MRI muscle quality only moderately predicts contracture severity so tendon and joint contributions are unquantified; glucocorticoid therapy and ambulation loss co-evolve with contracture; and cerebral palsy, spina bifida, and orthopedic contracture causes overlap the differential.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: immobilization and positioning contractures in nonambulatory patients
orthopedic and post-surgical contracture (the published joint-replacement-residuals contracture window, not recycled per ME-29)
upper-motor-neuron contracture in cerebral palsy (the published cerebral-palsy window)
burn scar contracture (the published burns window)
arthritis-related stiffness

evidenceGaps: No located cohort separates dystrophy-driven shortening from immobilization and positioning effects; MRI muscle quality only moderately predicts contracture severity so tendon and joint contributions are unquantified; glucocorticoid therapy and ambulation loss co-evolve with contracture; and cerebral palsy, spina bifida, and orthopedic contracture causes overlap the differential.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on the disease-sequela precedent with the subtype-scope limit carried openly: the 178-boy longitudinal Duchenne cohort found contracture prevalence and severity increasing with age and tracking ambulatory decline (PMID 35124659) and the maturation-corrected trajectory study documented dorsiflexion range-of-motion decline of 0.23-0.33 z-score per year alongside muscle size loss (PMID 40100909); because both anchors are Duchenne-specific cohorts where glucocorticoid exposure and immobilization co-evolve and muscle imaging only moderately predicts contracture, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and routes individual claims through dated range-of-motion assessment with immobilization, orthopedic, and neurologic exclusion.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies document scoliosis at population-based and natural-history level: the US MD STARnet population-based study of 513 analysed dystrophinopathy individuals found approximately one-quarter with curvature of at least 20 degrees and loss of independent ambulation carrying adjusted hazards of curvature 6.2 to 31.6 across Cobb thresholds, with non-use of corticosteroids associated with higher hazards (PMID 34787322), and the 105-patient natural-history review found scoliosis developing in 95 percent of patients after loss of ambulation with curve direction determined by asymmetric iliotibial band contracture and spinal orthoses failing to control progression in 94 percent (PMID 3611341); the relationship is recorded as documented disease-sequela association only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: the anchors are dystrophinopathy cohorts where scoliosis follows ambulation loss and asymmetric soft-tissue contracture, so whether any individual curve is attributable to the dystrophy requires individual orthopedic attribution with idiopathic, neuromuscular, and congenital exclusion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Progressive paraspinal and pelvic girdle muscle degeneration with asymmetric contracture (documented iliotibial band asymmetry) drives unbalanced spinal loading so neuromuscular scoliosis results and progresses after ambulation loss, the asymmetric-balance route stated in the natural-history review and consistent with the ambulation-loss hazard gradient, but whether this route produced any individual curve remains hypothesized until radiographic and functional records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at population-based surveillance plus retrospective natural-history class only: the MD STARnet analysis covers curvature data for 513 of 1,054 ascertained individuals with radiograph ascertainment varying, the 105-patient review is a 1987-era cohort predating modern corticosteroid and exon-skipping practice, and corticosteroid use is associated with lower curve hazards so treatment materially alters the course.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: No located cohort reports scoliosis incidence under modern glucocorticoid-first management; radiograph ascertainment was incomplete in the population-based study; the natural-history cohort predates current therapy; brace management has documented poor efficacy in this population; and idiopathic adolescent scoliosis, congenital vertebral anomalies, and other neuromuscular causes compete for individual attribution.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: idiopathic adolescent scoliosis
scoliosis in cerebral palsy (the published cerebral-palsy scoliosis window, not recycled per ME-29)
congenital vertebral malformation
scoliosis in other neuromuscular disease (spina bifida, Friedreich ataxia)
osteoporotic vertebral fracture-related deformity (the companion osteoporosis pathway)

evidenceGaps: No located cohort reports scoliosis incidence under modern glucocorticoid-first management; radiograph ascertainment was incomplete in the population-based study; the natural-history cohort predates current therapy; brace management has documented poor efficacy in this population; and idiopathic adolescent scoliosis, congenital vertebral anomalies, and other neuromuscular causes compete for individual attribution.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on the disease-sequela precedent with the treatment-era limit carried openly: the MD STARnet population-based study found one-quarter of 513 dystrophinopathy individuals with curvature at least 20 degrees and ambulation loss carrying curvature hazards of 6.2-31.6 (PMID 34787322), and the 105-patient review found scoliosis in 95 percent after ambulation loss with asymmetric iliotibial band contracture determining curve direction (PMID 3611341); because the natural-history cohort predates modern corticosteroid practice (with steroid non-use associated with higher hazards) and radiograph ascertainment was incomplete, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and routes individual claims through dated radiographic assessment with idiopathic, congenital, and other neuromuscular exclusion.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies document dilated cardiomyopathy at adult-cohort and registry level: the adult DMD clinic cohort of 33 patients states cardiomyopathy is universally penetrant in young adults with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and is increasingly the preponderant cause of death, documenting declining left ventricular ejection fraction (51 percent at enrollment to 45 percent at follow-up) and midwall fibrosis on cardiac MRI (PMID 42112505), the European HOPE-MD registry of 274 adults with genetically confirmed DMD or Becker muscular dystrophy and ejection fraction at or below 40 percent frames both dystrophinopathies as often progressing to dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure (PMID 42169468), and the state-of-the-art CMR review documents inferolateral subepicardial fibrosis as a dystrophinopathy signature with subclinical myocardial involvement years before overt dysfunction (PMID 41548716); the relationship is recorded as documented disease-sequela association only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: the anchors are genotype-confirmed dystrophinopathy cohorts but the cardiomyopathy penetrance varies with age, genotype, and treatment era, so whether any individual cardiomyopathy is attributable to the dystrophy requires individual cardiology attribution with hypertensive, inflammatory, and familial exclusion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Dystrophin-deficient cardiomyocyte membrane instability drives progressive myocyte necrosis with fibrofatty replacement (the inferolateral subepicardial fibrosis CMR signature) so dilated cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction result, the fibrofatty-degeneration route documented by the CMR tissue-characterization literature and the declining-ejection-fraction cohort trajectory, modified by afterload and treatment exposure, but whether this route produced any individual cardiomyopathy remains hypothesized until imaging and genotype records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at single-center adult cohort plus disease-registry class only: the 33-patient cohort is one adult clinic with high rates of failed imaging, the HOPE-MD registry is conditioned on ejection fraction at or below 40 percent so it cannot estimate penetrance, and modern cardioprotective therapy initiated before ejection-fraction decline materially changes the natural history.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: No located cohort reports age-specific cardiomyopathy penetrance under contemporary early-cardioprotection protocols; the registry is conditioned on established systolic dysfunction; CMR completion was only 25 percent in the adult cohort because of positioning limitations; genotype-phenotype variation between Duchenne and Becker is unmodeled; and hypertensive, tachycardia-mediated, and familial cardiomyopathies compete for individual attribution.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: hypertensive heart disease (the published hypertension window)
tachycardia-induced and myocarditic cardiomyopathy
familial dilated cardiomyopathy
congestive heart failure from other causes (the cardiomyopathy identity's published heart-failure window is an intermediate-node pathway not recycled per ME-29)
diabetic and ischemic cardiomyopathy

evidenceGaps: No located cohort reports age-specific cardiomyopathy penetrance under contemporary early-cardioprotection protocols; the registry is conditioned on established systolic dysfunction; CMR completion was only 25 percent in the adult cohort because of positioning limitations; genotype-phenotype variation between Duchenne and Becker is unmodeled; and hypertensive, tachycardia-mediated, and familial cardiomyopathies compete for individual attribution.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on the disease-sequela precedent with the penetrance-timing limit carried openly: the adult DMD cohort of 33 patients documents universally penetrant young-adult cardiomyopathy with ejection-fraction decline and midwall fibrosis (PMID 42112505), the HOPE-MD registry of 274 genotype-confirmed adults frames progression to dilated cardiomyopathy (PMID 42169468), and the CMR review documents subclinical myocardial involvement years before overt dysfunction (PMID 41548716); because the registry is conditioned on established systolic dysfunction and early cardioprotection alters the course, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and routes individual claims through dated echocardiography/CMR and genotype review with hypertensive, inflammatory, and familial exclusion.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Duchenne muscular dystrophy documents obstructive sleep apnea at polysomnographic cohort and review level: the prospective polysomnography study of 12 consecutive Duchenne males found obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in 42 percent by PSG versus none of eight controls (p=0.004), with 58 percent reporting at least one apnea-related symptom and cardiac autonomic dysfunction more pronounced with apnea (PMID 32740854), and the sleep-disordered-breathing review documents young patients at risk of obstructive apneas through weight gain from inactivity and prolonged corticosteroid therapy while older patients hypoventilate from respiratory muscle weakness (PMID 28397169); the relationship is recorded as documented disease-sequela association only, scoped to the obstructive signal.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: the polysomnographic anchor is 12 boys and the review describes mixed obstructive and hypoventilatory phenotypes, so whether any individual apnea is attributable to the dystrophy requires individual sleep-study attribution with obesity, tonsillar, and central-apnea exclusion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Progressive pharyngeal and upper-airway muscle weakness with corticosteroid-associated weight gain drives sleep-related upper-airway collapse so obstructive apneas result, the collapse route consistent with the PSG-documented obstructive events in young Duchenne males and the review's weight-gain and muscle-weakness framing, but whether this route produced any individual apnea remains hypothesized until polysomnographic records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at small prospective PSG cohort plus narrative review class only: the polysomnographic anchor is 12 consecutive males with 8 controls, the review mixes obstructive phenotypes in the young with hypoventilation phenotypes in the older (the latter outside the sleep-apnea identity's obstructive scope), and no located cohort quantifies apnea incidence across the dystrophinopathy age span.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: No located cohort quantifies obstructive sleep apnea incidence in a large dystrophinopathy population; the small PSG cohort is single-center; obstructive and hypoventilatory sleep-disordered breathing overlap in this population and only the obstructive component is in scope; corticosteroid-era weight trajectories are unmodeled; and obesity, craniofacial, and adenotonsillar causes of apnea compete in the same young population.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: hypoventilation from diaphragmatic weakness (the review's older-patient phenotype, outside the obstructive scope of this edge)
obstructive sleep apnea from obesity or adenotonsillar hypertrophy independent of the dystrophy
central sleep apnea
nocturia-related sleep disruption
cardiac arrhythmia-related nocturnal symptoms (the cardiomyopathy pathway)

evidenceGaps: No located cohort quantifies obstructive sleep apnea incidence in a large dystrophinopathy population; the small PSG cohort is single-center; obstructive and hypoventilatory sleep-disordered breathing overlap in this population and only the obstructive component is in scope; corticosteroid-era weight trajectories are unmodeled; and obesity, craniofacial, and adenotonsillar causes of apnea compete in the same young population.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at small PSG-cohort class with the obstructive-scope limit carried openly: the prospective polysomnography study found obstructive sleep apnea in 42 percent of 12 Duchenne males versus none of controls (PMID 32740854) and the sleep-disordered-breathing review attributes young-patient obstructive apneas to weight gain and upper-airway muscle weakness (PMID 28397169); because the anchor cohort is small and the review's hypoventilation phenotype falls outside the sleep-apnea identity's obstructive scope, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and routes individual claims through dated polysomnography with obesity, tonsillar, and central-apnea exclusion.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Duchenne muscular dystrophy documents swallowing dysfunction at adult cohort and orofacial-database level: the 48-patient adult cohort study found abnormal swallowing quality-of-life scores in 33 of 48 patients (69 percent) with independent predictors age, maximal inspiratory pressure, and autonomic symptoms, describing dysphagia as a common but often overlooked symptom attributable to progressive deterioration of swallowing muscle groups (PMID 37212070), and the national orofacial database study of 206 individuals with 21 congenital or childhood-onset neuromuscular disorders found orofacial dysfunction in 70 percent overall and in 100 percent of the 19-49-year-old Duchenne subgroup (PMID 42142020); the relationship is recorded as documented disease-sequela association only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: the anchors measure swallowing quality of life and orofacial screening profiles rather than instrumental swallow diagnoses, so whether any individual dysphagia is attributable to the dystrophy requires individual videofluoroscopic attribution with medication, reflux, and neurologic exclusion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Progressive neuromuscular degeneration of oropharyngeal and inspiratory muscle groups drives loss of swallow pressure and coordination so oropharyngeal dysphagia results, the myopathic-degeneration route stated in the adult cohort (maximal inspiratory pressure under 22 predicted altered swallowing quality of life with 92 percent accuracy) and consistent with the orofacial-dysfunction predominance, but whether this route produced any individual dysphagia remains hypothesized until videofluoroscopic records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at single adult cohort plus registry-database class only: the 48-patient study measures SWAL-QOL patient-reported outcomes rather than instrumental swallow diagnosis, the orofacial database mixes 21 neuromuscular disorders with the Duchenne subgroup small, and noninvasive ventilation use in the cohort normalizes blood gases and may mask the respiratory contribution to swallow safety.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: No located cohort reports videofluoroscopically confirmed dysphagia incidence in Duchenne muscular dystrophy; patient-reported swallowing quality of life is not diagnosis; the adult cohort's predictors conflate inspiratory weakness with swallow mechanics; and medication effects, gastroesophageal reflux, and brainstem pathology are competing dysphagia causes.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: oropharyngeal weakness in ALS (the published als dysphagia window, not recycled per ME-29)
gastroesophageal reflux and esophageal dysmotility
medication- and sedation-related dysphagia
obstructive oral-pharyngeal pathology
cognitive or brainstem causes of dysphagia

evidenceGaps: No located cohort reports videofluoroscopically confirmed dysphagia incidence in Duchenne muscular dystrophy; patient-reported swallowing quality of life is not diagnosis; the adult cohort's predictors conflate inspiratory weakness with swallow mechanics; and medication effects, gastroesophageal reflux, and brainstem pathology are competing dysphagia causes.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at adult-cohort plus registry-database class with the outcome-measure limit carried openly: the 48-patient adult Duchenne cohort found abnormal swallowing quality of life in 69 percent with inspiratory-pressure predictors (PMID 37212070) and the 206-person orofacial database found dysfunction in all 19-49-year-old Duchenne participants (PMID 42142020); because the anchors measure patient-reported and screening outcomes rather than instrumental swallow diagnosis and the als window keeps its own evidence (ME-29), the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only and routes individual claims through videofluoroscopy with reflux, medication, and neurologic exclusion.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Duchenne muscular dystrophy documents osteoporosis at large routine-imaging cohort and risk-factor study level: the 9-year retrospective cohort of 408 Duchenne patients on daily glucocorticoids undergoing routine spine imaging found osteoporosis prevalence rising progressively with age (4.4, 20.9, and 58.3 percent at ages 5, 10, and 18) and long-bone or vertebral fracture prevalence of 16.5, 37.4, and 83.3 percent at the same ages (PMID 41912872), and the cross-sectional risk-factor study of males aged 4-25 found markers of systemic glucocorticoid exposure (shorter stature, greater bone age delay, lower lumbar spine bone density) associated with prevalent vertebral fractures (PMID 36342539); the relationship is recorded as documented disease-and-treatment-sequela association only.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual: both anchors attribute bone disease jointly to glucocorticoid exposure, muscle weakness, and restricted mobility, so whether any individual osteoporosis is attributable to the dystrophy versus its treatment requires individual densitometric and endocrine attribution with hypogonadism, vitamin-D, and immobilization exclusion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure with progressive immobility and muscle-driven unloading of bone drives suppressed bone formation and accumulating vertebral fragility so osteoporosis and fractures result, the combined treatment-and-disuse route consistent with the age-and-exposure dose pattern and the glucocorticoid-marker risk gradient, but whether this route produced any individual osteoporosis remains hypothesized until densitometry and exposure records are reviewed.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The association is supported at single-center retrospective imaging cohort plus cross-sectional risk-factor class only: all 408 cohort patients were on daily glucocorticoids so the untreated natural history is unobserved, the risk-factor study is cross-sectional with prevalent (not incident) fractures, and low total-body bone density preceding detectable osteoporosis complicates timing attribution.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: No located cohort separates glucocorticoid from immobility contributions or reports bone outcomes in untreated dystrophinopathy; the imaging cohort is single-center retrospective; fracture prevalence figures reflect cumulative vertebral accrual; hypogonadism and vitamin-D deficiency overlap the population; and glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis in other diseases (the published glucocorticoid window context) competes for individual attribution.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis from other therapies (treatment-mediation recorded, not an independent identity pathway)
disuse osteoporosis from immobilization independent of the dystrophy
hypogonadism-related bone loss (the published hypogonadism osteoporosis window, not recycled per ME-29)
vitamin-D deficiency and malnutrition-related low bone density
idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis

evidenceGaps: No located cohort separates glucocorticoid from immobility contributions or reports bone outcomes in untreated dystrophinopathy; the imaging cohort is single-center retrospective; fracture prevalence figures reflect cumulative vertebral accrual; hypogonadism and vitamin-D deficiency overlap the population; and glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis in other diseases (the published glucocorticoid window context) competes for individual attribution.
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY on the disease-and-treatment-sequela precedent with the treatment-mediation limit carried openly: the 408-patient routine-imaging cohort found osteoporosis prevalence rising from 4.4 to 58.3 percent between ages 5 and 18 with fracture prevalence rising from 16.5 to 83.3 percent (PMID 41912872) and the risk-factor study linked glucocorticoid-exposure markers to prevalent vertebral fractures (PMID 36342539); because all cohort patients were on daily glucocorticoids and immobility co-evolves, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only with a MULTIFACTORIAL mechanism naming both documented contributors, and routes individual claims through dated densitometry with hypogonadism, vitamin-D, and immobilization exclusion.

sourceReferences.citation: Nasomyont N, Tian C, Hornung L, et al. The burden of bone disease in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: age-specific prevalence of osteoporosis and low bone density Osteoporos Int. 2026 May;37(5):1319-1328. doi: 10.1007/s00198-026-07963-1. PMID 41912872.
sourceReferences.note: 9-year retrospective cohort of 408 DMD patients (mean age 8) on daily glucocorticoids with routine annual spine radiographs and DXA: osteoporosis prevalence 4.4%, 20.9%, 58.3% at ages 5, 10, 18; long-bone/vertebral fracture prevalence 16.5%, 37.4%, 83.3%; low total-body BMD preceded clinically detectable osteoporosis; supports the bounded disease-and-treatment association only.
